# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about the way light falls through a kitchen window at four in the afternoon. Not in a poetic sense, though perhaps it is poetic—I mean the actual, physical phenomenon of it. How the angle changes with the seasons, how dust particles become suddenly visible in the beam, how a glass of water on the counter transforms into something radiant and inexplicable when the light passes through it.

There's something profoundly unsettling about noticing things you've seen a thousand times before. It's like the universe is playing a prank on you, revealing that you've been living inside a mystery the whole time. You walk past the same corner store for months, maybe years, and then one day you actually *see* it—the specific shade of green on its awning, the way the letters of its sign are slightly uneven, the crack in the window shaped like a lightning bolt. How was it there all along? How did you miss it?

I think this is what people mean when they talk about "being present." It's not some New Age construct, though it's been marketed that way. It's just the shock of reality asserting itself. The world is far stranger and more detailed than we give it credit for, and we're mostly just sleepwalking through it, our brains extracting only the minimum information necessary to accomplish our tasks and get to the next thing.

Consider the human hand. I don't mean this in the way art school students mean it, struggling to draw hands correctly. I mean actually look at your own hand right now. Look at the specific geography of the veins on the back of it, the way the light creates tiny shadows in the creases of your knuckles, the fact that you have five digits of subtly different lengths and thicknesses, each one capable of exerting different amounts of force and pressure. There are tendons under your skin that you can feel move if you flex your fingers while touching your wrist. There are nerve endings so sensitive that you can feel a single grain of sand between two fingertips. Your hands are constantly in contact with the world, constantly gathering information about texture and temperature, and you almost never think about them at all.

I read once that some people become deeply anxious when they think too hard about their own bodies, about the fact that they're piloting around a collection of organs in a bag of skin. But I've found it to be the opposite—the more attention I pay to the actual, specific details of embodied existence, the less anxious I feel. There's something grounding about it. It's like a reset button for the mind.

Maybe this is why people garden, or do woodworking, or cook with attention. These activities have become somewhat romanticized lately, marketed as wellness practices or aesthetic lifestyle choices. But I think the real point isn't the aspirational Instagram photographs of heirloom tomatoes or sourdough bread. The real point is that you're engaged in something where your attention naturally focuses on the specific and material. You can't think about three other things while you're kneading bread dough because the texture in your hands demands your presence. You can't worry about abstract problems while you're tending plants because the plants are presenting concrete problems—this one needs water, that one is getting leggy, this other one is being attacked by aphids.

There's a book I keep returning to called "The Poetics of Space" by Gaston Bachelard. It's a strange, dreamlike book that's mostly about how we relate psychologically to the spaces we inhabit. He writes about houses and rooms and cupboards and cellars, but not in a literal architectural way. He's interested in how spaces feel, what they mean, how they shape us. He has this lovely passage about intimate immensity—the idea that small, enclosed spaces can somehow feel vast and infinite when you're truly present in them. A corner of a room, a window seat, a small study. He writes about how we project ourselves into spaces and how spaces project themselves into us.

I thought about this recently while sitting in a coffee shop. Not a trendy coffee shop with exposed brick and Edison bulbs and a curated soundtrack—just a regular, slightly tired-looking place on a regular street. The kind of place that exists primarily for people to buy coffee, not for people to perform the aesthetic of buying coffee. The espresso machine was old and hissed when it steamed milk. The barista was moving with the kind of efficient weariness that comes from doing the same things hundreds of times. The other people there weren't posing for invisible cameras; they were checking email, or working on laptops, or just sitting and thinking, the way people do in these liminal spaces that are neither home nor work nor completely public but something in between.

And I realized that the coffee shop, in its ordinariness, was exactly what I needed. Not because it was Instagram-worthy or because I was performing some kind of identity by being there, but because it was a space where I could simply exist without explanation. No one cared who I was. I didn't have to justify my presence. I could sit and drink coffee and watch the light change outside the window and think about whatever I wanted to think about, and it was fine.

This is something that's increasingly rare, I think. Most spaces are designed to extract something from you now—your attention, your money, your data, your eyeballs for advertisements. The default state of existing in the world has become transactional. Even spaces that are ostensibly free—public parks, libraries, sidewalks—are watched and measured and analyzed in various ways. We're always being counted, always being evaluated. The coffee shop, too, in its own small way, but at least it was honest about it. You buy coffee, you sit down, that's the entire contract.

I've become fascinated lately by things that are disappearing or have already disappeared. Not in a nostalgic way, though maybe there's some of that too. I mean things like payphones, or the specific visual texture of older neighborhoods before they're gentrified and homogenized, or the particular feeling of boredom that children used to experience before they had constant access to entertainment. These things aren't inherently better than their replacements. I'm not yearning for some imagined past. But there was something about their specific qualities that offered something to human experience that's harder to find now.

Boredom is interesting to think about. We've been taught to view it as a negative state, something to be escaped as quickly as possible. But I wonder if boredom is actually the mental space where certain kinds of thinking and imagination become possible. If you're never bored, if there's always stimulation available, if you're never left alone with just your own thoughts, what does that do to the way your mind develops? There's research suggesting that attention spans are decreasing, that the constant stimulus is fragmenting our ability to focus. But I think it might be more fundamental than that. I think it might be changing the way we think about what's interesting in the first place.

A person who has spent time being bored, truly bored, without escape routes, might develop a different relationship to the world. They might find interest in things that aren't inherently exciting—in the grain of wood, in the way water moves, in the specific acoustic properties of their own neighborhood. They might have learned to generate their own meaning from the ordinary world rather than waiting for it to be provided to them.

There's a Buddhist concept called "bare attention"—the idea of noticing what's actually present without adding layers of judgment or narrative. Just seeing what is. This sounds simple but is actually quite difficult, because the human mind is constantly adding stories to everything. We see a person on the street and immediately construct narratives about them. We have an emotion and immediately identify it and construct a story about why we have it. We see an object and classify it and move on. Actually paying attention to what's in front of you, without all these added layers, requires deliberate effort.

But here's what's interesting: when you do manage it, even briefly, things become strange and compelling again. A tree is not just a tree—it's this specific tree, with these specific proportions and this specific way of growing and this specific pattern of light and shadow falling on its leaves. A person is not just a representative of a category—they're a specific arrangement of features and movements and expressions that's unique to them. Reality becomes vivid.

I think this is partly why people get interested in photography. A camera is a tool for directing attention, for saying "look at this." And when you look at a good photograph, you're looking at what someone else chose to notice and considered worth preserving. It's like they're saying, I found this moment interesting; let me show you why it might be interesting to you too. And sometimes it works, and you see something familiar transformed by someone else's attention, and it's jarring.

The same is true of writing, of course, though writing works differently because it can layer language on top of what's observed. You can use language to reach toward something that might not be visible in the image itself—the feeling of the moment, the context, the way something fits into a larger pattern. Writing is like giving someone else permission to look more carefully, and then also giving them the words to think with while they look.

This is what I love about good writing, whether it's literary fiction or essays or even just a well-written article about something mundane. It's someone saying, I looked at this thing carefully, and here's what I found. And then when you read it, you become able to look at the world that way too, at least for a little while. The author has trained your attention.

I've been reading a lot of Annie Dillard lately, partly because she seems to be fundamentally interested in how to pay attention to the world. She writes about light and vision and the act of looking with this intensity that borders on obsessive. But it's not a detached, clinical observation. There's always joy in it, always a kind of active love for the thing being looked at. She'll describe the way light moves through a prism or how water reflects the sky with the kind of wonder that makes you realize you've been taking these things for granted.

And the thing is, once you've read something like that, you can't quite unsee it. You'll walk past a window and see how the light is hitting it differently, and you'll think of Dillard, and you'll notice it in a way you wouldn't have before. This is how culture works, I think. It's a constant conversation between people about what's worth paying attention to, what's worth caring about, what matters.

I think we need more of this, or a different kind of it. Not the version of attention that technology companies have monetized, where your attention is valuable because it can be sold to advertisers. But the kind of attention where you and reality are in direct relationship, where you notice what's actually there and let it affect you. Where you allow yourself to be changed by what you're looking at.

This might sound like I'm being critical of technology, but I don't think I am, really. Technology is just a tool, and like all tools, it amplifies certain human tendencies and diminishes others. We're always making these trade-offs. Writing allowed people to record and share ideas across time and space, but it also changed how our brains developed, how we think. Photography and film allowed us to see things in new ways, but they also created this culture of capturing experience rather than experiencing it directly. The internet connects us to vast amounts of information but fragments our attention.

The question isn't whether technology is good or bad. The question is what we do with it, what we choose to pay attention to, how we structure our lives and our attention. We can use technology to make it easier to notice and share the strange beauty of ordinary things. Or we can use it to avoid noticing anything at all.

I think I'm going to look at my hands again now, actually. I notice I've been sitting in one position while writing this and my hand is starting to feel a little cramped. That's a specific sensation—the tightness, the slight pain, the awareness of my own body reasserting itself. And that's interesting too. That's real. That's now.
